extracted.intended_audience: students, statesmen, and readers interested in constitutional design and the stability of republics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative criteria for constitution design and for diagnosing causes of degeneration in republics (e.g., how to prevent oligarchy, democracy→tyranny, and preserve the laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of permanent laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of permanent laws, to restrain the passions and vices of men, and to secure to the citizens the blessings of society, in the peaceable enjoyment of their lives, liberties, and properties
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws must be treated as the master, guardian, and friend of every citizen; citizens should appeal to the laws when deprived of rights. Permanent laws restrain private passions that otherwise disrupt society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of different orders with opposite powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of different orders of men, with various and opposite powers, prerogatives, and privileges, to watch over one another, to balance each other, and to compel each other at all times to be real guardians of the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A durable constitution requires multiple distinct bodies (monarchical, aristocratical, democratical) that check and balance each other so that no single order can subvert the laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the laws as primary remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every citizen must look up to the laws, as his master, his guardian, and his friend; whenever any fellow-citizen attempts to deprive him of his right, he must appeal to the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political or personal conflicts should be channeled through legal institutions rather than private retaliation; this principle underpins institutional checks (appeal mechanisms between orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three divisions of power (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Without three divisions of power, stationed to watch each other, and compare each other's conduct with the laws, it will be impossible that the laws would at all times preserve their authority, and govern all men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixed constitution—incorporating monarchical, aristocratical, and democratical elements—is recommended for resilience; the specific institutional forms may vary but must enable mutual restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardianship/appeal mechanisms to prevent aristocracy→oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The aristocracy, or ambitious republic, becomes immediately an oligarchy—How shall it be prevented? Place two guardians of the laws to watch the aristocracy: one, in the shape of a king, on one side of it; another, in the shape of a democratical assembly, on the other side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions so that an aristocratic order has both a monarchical and a popular counterweight; institutional allies/appeal routes deter consolidation of oligarchic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for oligarchy→democracy degeneration
rubrics_metrics.description: The oligarchy, become a democracy — How shall it be prevented? By giving the natural aristocracy in society its rational and just weight, and by giving it a regal power to appeal to, against the madness of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When oligarchic tendencies produce populist overturns, provide legal and institutional resources (e.g., regal/peer appeals) for the aristocratic element to check unjust popular measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing democracy→tyranny by institutional allies
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy becomes a tyranny—How shall this be prevented? By giving it an able independent ally in an aristocratical assembly, with whom it may unite against the unjust and illegal designs of any one man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An independent aristocratic body can moderate democratic excesses and block the rise of a single demagogic leader; durable checks require independent institutions rather than ephemeral majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of executive from legislative and judicial powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power was not separated from the legislative; nor the different parts of the legislature properly divided or balanced: the executive power and judicial were both chiefly in legislative hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrating executive and judicial authority within the legislature undermines balance; institutional design should separate functions to avoid domination by a single branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal qualifications (wealth) for senators to secure dignity and resist corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws, which, requiring a large fortune for every senator and public officer, in order to support his dignity, and secure him against the temptations to corruption, confined the choice to the first families and abilities united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property qualifications were intended as a check against corruption by ensuring officeholders could sustain public dignity; but such requirements trade off inclusiveness and may exclude able but poorer men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimity rule with appeal to the people as democratic check
rubrics_metrics.description: The senate should always be unanimous; and if any one senator insisted upon his own opinion against all the rest, there could be no decision, but by an appeal to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A unanimity rule with an appeal-to-people clause injects a democratic element into elite bodies, but it also tilts the constitution toward popular influence; organizers must weigh stability versus popular recourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional oversight committees to check elites (Carthage's committee of 104 & council of five)
rubrics_metrics.description: A committee of one hundred and four members of the senate, appointed to watch the ambition of the great families ... a sub-committee of five ... their office was for life; they filled up vacancies out of the one hundred and four ... they had the supreme tribunal of criminal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent oversight organs that review magistrates and generals can restrain elite ambition; however, lifetime appointment and self-perpetuation can become unpopular and destabilizing if later made elective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of converting lifetime/insulated offices into elective ones
rubrics_metrics.description: It grew unpopular; and the law which at last made it annual and elective, probably laid the foundation of the ruin of the commonwealth, by changing the balance, and introducing the dominatio plebis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transforming insulating institutions (life offices) into short-term elective bodies can upset the established balance and empower transient majorities; institutional reforms must consider long-run equilibrium effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks must be natural and effective, not merely formal
rubrics_metrics.description: All the checks ... although they preserved the state five hundred years, could not prolong its period above seven hundred; because, after all, the balance was not natural, nor effectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design checks that function in practice (natural incentives, power-sharing) rather than relying solely on formal arrangements which can be circumvented or eroded over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume commerce inevitably corrupts manners
rubrics_metrics.description: With all their acknowledged eagerness for money, this people were so many centuries untainted with luxury and venality; and preserved their primitive frugality of manners, and integrity in elections. This ... may lead us to doubt the universality of the doctrine, that commerce corrupts manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy prescriptions about commerce and morality should be empirically grounded; commercial wealth does not necessarily produce corruption if institutions and civic norms sustain integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional patron-client arrangements can sustain harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution by which every plebeian was allowed to choose any patrician for his patron, introduced an intercourse of good offices between these orders, made the patricians emulate each other in acts of civility and humanity to their clients, and contributed to preserve the peace and harmony of Rome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms fostering mutual obligations between social orders (patronage, clientage) can moderate conflict and bind elites to public obligations, helping maintain long periods without civil bloodshed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and process of tyrant formation from democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Out of no other republic is tyranny constituted but out of democracy; and out of the most excessive liberty, the greatest and most savage slavery. ... He now becomes seditious towards those who have substance, and when he fails he goes against his enemies with open force, and becomes an accomplished tyrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for excessive liberty, demagogic leaders who curry favor with the masses, abolition of debts and division of lands as populist ploys, creation of personal guards, persecution of elites, and use of war/poverty to render citizens dependent—these are red flags of imminent tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral pattern of established tyrants
rubrics_metrics.description: The president of a city, thus not behaving like a truly great man, tumbles down many others, and sits in his chair a consummate tyrant ... he frees from debts, distributes lands, promises many things, then raises wars so that the people may want a leader; he must cut off all those who are of a more manly spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tyrant consolidates power by appearing mild initially, distributing favors, then eliminating rivals and creating dependence through wars and economic strain; institutional designers should create safeguards against these sequential tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of tyrannical government
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the city and the tyrant shall be slavish, poor, timorous; and you will find more lamentations and groans, weepings and torments, than in any other city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate regimes not only by outward grandeur but by the wellbeing and liberty of citizens; tyranny produces pervasive misery despite ostensible power or magnificence.
